interest: 1930s fears of Japanese spying near the Gulf of Fonseca.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.20216) covers U.S. diplomatic and intelligence surveillance of alleged Japanese espionage, topographical surveying, and commercial maritime activities in El Salvador and neighboring Central American republics between 1932 and 1935. Triggered by a confidential request from the Director of Naval Intelligence in January 1932 regarding reports of Japanese individuals posing as fishermen to carry out covert surveys along Latin American coasts, the file tracks inquiries conducted by the U.S. Legation in San Salvador under Chargé d'Affaires William J. McCafferty and Minister Frank P. Corrigan. While initial diplomatic inquiries found no evidence of illicit coastal surveys, subsequent documentation in 1933 and 1935 records persistent concerns over Japanese requests for commercial fishing concessions in Salvadoran waters and prominent Central American press reports detailing the suspicious movements of two alleged Japanese Ministry of War agents, S. Mijuo and T. Furuta, around the Gulf of Fonseca.
